name: Iris Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Iris. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. I'm going to describe five pictures of how AI might change work and ask how you'd react. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yes, that's fine. I'm Iris, I'm 43. My husband Yusuf has a small building firm, and three years ago, when our youngest started school, I joined it on the tools. Before that I was home with the children for twelve years, and before that I worked in a bakery.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. Before the pictures, tell me about a normal working day for you. What do you actually do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We do house extensions, garages, and a lot of repairs on old houses in the villages round us. There's Yusuf, his cousin Hamid, an apprentice called Ryan, and me. I'm on studwork, roof battens, fixing plasterboard, and I do the tidying and ordering because nobody else will. I love working next to my husband, which people find strange, and I love when a family moves into the room we built. What wears me out is lifting the plasterboard, and being the one still learning when I'm the boss's wife.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, thank God, people can stop worrying and get back to work. I'd say it at our congregation's coffee morning, where everyone talks about it. And I'd say the computer is useful for quotes, but it doesn't build anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For us it means the business carries on. Yusuf's spent fifteen years building a name in the villages, people ring him because their neighbour did. Nobody's going to ask a chat app round for tea and then give it the job of building their kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd keep going as we are. Yusuf might buy the second van he's been talking about and take on another apprentice. I'd keep learning, and keep using the AI on my phone now and then to plan the week's deliveries, since Yusuf showed me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Grateful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you feel about joining the firm at forty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous. My hands were soft from baking and childcare, and the first month I cried in the van twice. But it's our family's business, and I'd rather it was me than paying a stranger. Now I can fix a ceiling as well as Ryan, nearly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the business mean to your family, beyond money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's everything. It paid for our house and the little cottage we rent out, and Adam already says he'll take it over one day. It's our name on the van, Usman Builders, and that means something.

S0.say: I'd say thank God, people can stop worrying and get back to work. Computers help with quotes but don't build anything.
S0.think: She thinks the family business carries on, because people hire builders through neighbours and trust. Nobody gives a chat app the job of building their kitchen.
S0.do: Keeps working in the family firm while her husband considers a second van and another apprentice. Uses AI on her phone now and then to plan deliveries.
S0.quote: Nobody's going to ask a chat app round for tea and then give it the job of building their kitchen.
S0.fieldNote: Iris's whole world is the family firm, with their name on the van and the house and rental cottage it paid for. She joined late and found it hard but is proud of her progress. She uses AI a little because her husband showed her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say small family firms like ours need a fair chance, not just the big companies with all the new machines. I'd say keep apprenticeships going. I wouldn't want the government taking over, just being fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd worry about the big firms. If they get robots that do extensions faster and cheaper, people might go with them over a family firm. I don't worry about the robot taking my job. I worry about it taking Yusuf's customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once other small builders were using the new tools and they worked, we'd buy them, maybe the machine that cuts roof timbers or the software that does the drawings. I'd learn whatever we bought, I'm the one who reads the instructions. We'd put some of the savings into it, but carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A bit of worry about the business, not about the food on the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who decides, you or Yusuf, when it comes to buying new kit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He does, mostly, but he asks me. He'd buy every new tool he sees at the trade fair if I didn't stop him. I'm the one who says, let's wait until Hamid's brother has tried it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Adam, who wants to take over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to keep going, but to learn the computer side as well as the hammer. He's thirteen and he's better on the tablet than both of us. Maybe he's exactly what the firm will need.

S1.say: I'd say small family firms need a fair chance against big companies with new machines, and apprenticeships must continue. The government should be fair, not take over.
S1.think: She worries less about a robot taking her job than about big firms with robots taking her husband's customers.
S1.do: Buys new tools such as a roof-timber cutter or drawing software once other small builders have proved them, using savings carefully. Learns whatever the firm buys, as she's the one who reads instructions.
S1.feel: Uneasy about the business, not about food on the table.
S1.quote: I don't worry about the robot taking my job. I worry about it taking Yusuf's customers.
S1.fieldNote: Iris thinks as a business owner's partner rather than a junior worker: the threat is customers, not her own role. She's the brake on her husband's spending, waiting for proof. She sees her son's tablet skills as possibly what the firm needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not right to let it happen so fast, families and small firms need time. I'd say we need to look after each other. I wouldn't want people expecting the government to fix everything, but someone should slow this down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it would be the end of the firm, and the firm is everything we have. Fifteen years of Yusuf's name on that van, and in two years a robot does it cheaper. Every part of our income is in one basket, the business, and the basket would break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away, we'd stop the second van and the new apprentice. We'd talk about selling the business or the equipment while it's still worth something, maybe within the first year. We'd keep the rental cottage and the savings, and lean on Yusuf's brothers and our congregation if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd not sleep, and I'd be praying a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years isn't long. What would you be doing in those two years while you see it coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting out with something, honestly. Finishing the jobs we've got, not taking big ones, selling the vans and tools while other builders still want them. It's a horrible thing to plan, selling your husband's life's work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Yusuf the night you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make him tea and let him be quiet, he goes quiet when he's upset. Then I'd say, we built it once, we can build something else. I don't know if I'd believe it, but I'd say it.

S2.say: I'd say it's wrong to let this happen so fast because families and small firms need time. People should look after each other, and someone should slow it down without expecting government to fix everything.
S2.think: She thinks it would end the family firm, which holds all their income in one basket. Fifteen years of her husband's name on the van would be undercut by robots in two years.
S2.do: Stops the second van and new apprentice straight away and considers selling the business or equipment within the first year while it's worth something. Keeps the rental cottage and savings, and leans on family and her congregation if needed.
S2.feel: Alarmed, sleepless and praying a lot.
S2.quote: Fifteen years of Yusuf's name on that van, and in two years a robot does it cheaper.
S2.fieldNote: For Iris, AGI by 2028 threatens the family business that holds all their income, not just her job. She'd consider selling her husband's life's work while it still had value, which pained her to say. Her support system is family and faith, not government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for small businesses to adapt if they're sensible. I'd say help firms buy the new machines, not just the big ones. I'd say it at the coffee morning and to other builders' wives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives us a chance. If small firms like ours get the robots too, we keep the customers, because they know us. With five years, maybe we're the family firm that owns a robot, not the family firm a robot put out of business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, once a couple of other small builders had tried them, we'd buy the robot tools ourselves, a few at a time, using some savings. I'd learn to run them and Yusuf would do the customers, as he always has. We'd keep saving and keep the cottage as our safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but hopeful. There'd be a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years change for you, compared with the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the difference between selling up and changing. With two years, there's no time, everyone's caught. With five, a sensible firm can get ahead of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd learn to run the robots. Do you think you'd be good at it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm good at instructions and I'm patient. I'm not fast with a saw, but a robot doesn't need me to be fast with a saw. Funny if the thing that saves my place in the firm is a machine.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for sensible small businesses to adapt, and help should go to small firms buying machines, not just the big ones.
S3.think: She thinks five years gives them a chance to become the family firm that owns a robot instead of the one a robot puts out of business.
S3.do: Buys robot tools a few at a time with savings once other small builders have tried them. Learns to run them while her husband handles customers, keeping savings and the cottage as a safety net.
S3.feel: Anxious but hopeful, because there's a plan.
S3.quote: With five years, maybe we're the family firm that owns a robot, not the family firm a robot put out of business.
S3.fieldNote: The extra years change Iris's plan from selling up to adapting the firm. She sees her patience with instructions as more useful with robots than her slow saw work. Trust with local customers is the firm's edge in her view.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for any sensible family or business to get ready. I'd say keep apprenticeships so young people learn the craft before the robots. I'd say don't wait for the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time for a small firm. By then Adam would be 23, and maybe he takes over a business with machines in it. I'd want my son to inherit the firm, not a garage full of tools nobody needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd plan slowly: let other firms try things first, then buy what works. I'd do a proper course on the machines when they're common, maybe in year four or five. And I'd talk with Adam and Sara about what they want, and help Adam learn both sides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more peaceful than the other two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Sara, your youngest. What would you want for her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sara's eight and she wants to be a teacher, she teaches her dolls every evening. I'd say, good, children will always need someone who cares about them. A robot could probably teach her sums, but it couldn't make her feel clever the way her teacher does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change anything about how you see your own work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes me want to get properly good while it still matters. Maybe that sounds silly. But I'd like to have done it well, even for a short while, before the machines.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough for any sensible family or business to get ready, and apprenticeships should continue so young people learn the craft first. Don't wait for the government.
S4.think: She thinks ten years is long for a small firm and hopes her son inherits a business with machines in it, not a garage of useless tools.
S4.do: Lets other firms try new machines first, then buys what works, and takes a proper course on them around year four or five. Talks to both children about their futures and helps Adam learn both sides of the business.
S4.feel: Uneasy but more peaceful than the other two AGI pictures.
S4.quote: A robot could probably teach her sums, but it couldn't make her feel clever the way her teacher does.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Iris's thoughts turn to succession and her son inheriting a firm that still works. She wants to get properly good at the craft while it matters. Her daughter's love of teaching reassures her about people-centred work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: That's all five. Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because the whole family is in one business. What would help is time, and help for small firms to buy the machines so it's not only the big companies. And our families and congregation looking after each other, like they already do.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what it's like to work with your husband. It's lovely, mostly. If the firm went, I'd lose my job and my best days with him at the same time.

headlineQuote: I'd want my son to inherit the firm, not a garage full of tools nobody needs.
portrait: Iris Usman is a 43-year-old junior builder in her husband Yusuf's small family firm, which does extensions and old-house repairs in the villages. She worked in a bakery, stayed home with the children for twelve years, then joined the firm on the tools three years ago. The business, their house and a rental cottage make up the family's wealth, so she thinks like an owner and worries about customers more than her own role. She's traditional, faithful and careful, waiting for proof before buying new kit. She's calm about the plateau, uneasy about steady change, alarmed by AGI in two years because it would end the firm, and hopeful that more time lets them own the robots instead.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because all the family's income is in the one business, which would be finished.
whatWouldHelp: Time, help for small firms to buy machines alongside the big ones, and families and her congregation looking after each other.
